label: Idea
name: speech
summary:
Speech is the use of the human voice as a medium for language, combining vowel and consonant sounds to form words belonging to a language's lexicon. Spoken language is the primary and historically prior form of all human language — writing systems are later inventions that represent speech; for most of human history, all language was spoken. Speech is the defining cognitive achievement that separates Homo sapiens from all other animals.

The capacity for speech depends on a unique configuration of the human vocal tract, descended larynx, and the brain's left hemisphere language areas (Broca's area for speech production, Wernicke's area for comprehension). The evolution of these anatomical prerequisites is estimated at 300,000–100,000 years ago, coinciding with the emergence of behaviorally modern humans. The diversity of human speech — approximately 7,000 living languages — represents one of the most extraordinary examples of cultural variation in the natural world.

Speech has been the subject of intense philosophical inquiry since antiquity. Aristotle identified logos (reasoned speech) as the distinctive mark of the political animal; the Stoics analyzed the lekton (what is expressed by speech) as distinct from the physical sounds. In the 20th century, Ferdinand de Saussure's structural linguistics, J.L. Austin's speech act theory, and Noam Chomsky's generative grammar transformed the understanding of speech as a rule-governed cognitive system. The study of speech pathology, computational speech recognition, and the neural basis of language acquisition continues to be among the most active areas of cognitive science.

This fundamental cognitive achievement enabled early humans to communicate, cooperate, and ultimately shape their environment in ways that had far-reaching consequences for human history.

causes: Evolution of the descended human larynx and vocal tract anatomy (c. 300,000–100,000 years ago) enabling the range of sounds required for speech
Development of Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the left brain hemisphere providing the neural infrastructure for speech production and comprehension
Social complexity of early human groups creating selective pressure for communication beyond gesture and basic vocalizations
effects: All human languages — approximately 7,000 living languages — as elaborations of the universal capacity for speech
Writing systems developed as representations of speech, enabling the storage and transmission of knowledge across time
Philosophical and scientific investigation of language from Aristotle through Saussure and Chomsky transforming understanding of cognition
